##### Summary

Underwater image enhancement (UIE) research is trending toward heavy models, while lightweight alternatives are judged by parameters and FLOPs: proxies that say little about latency and energy on the edge accelerators underwater IoT platforms deploy. We report an on-device measurement study of shallow-water enhancement, whose per-channel attenuation physics favors compact quantized networks. Depthwise-separable U-Nets (9k-59k parameters) and a 4.3k-parameter curve model are trained on UIEB, quantized to FP16, INT8, and INT4 (palettized) with weight-only post-training quantization, and deployed via Core ML on the CPU, GPU, and Apple Neural Engine (ANE) of an Apple M3 Pro, with per-frame energy from idle-subtracted SoC power counters. The main 28.9k-parameter model at INT8 on the ANE enhances 256 × 256 frames at 945 FPS and 4.7 mJ/frame with no degradation at the reported two-decimal precision relative to FP16, and +3.2 dB PSNR over raw input on a 90-image held-out UIEB split. Across all 36 configurations on this FP16-compute stack, weight-only quantization provides no consistent latency or energy gain; energy is governed by compute-unit choice (3.6× vs. the GPU, 5.5-5.6× vs. the CPU) and network width. A W8A8 variant engages the ANE integer datapath (-18% latency, -28% energy at -0.37 dB), localizing the neutrality to weight-only PTQ rather than to the model or the NPU. A sub-30k-parameter network already saturates the measured quality-cost trade-off.

##### Summary

Learned image compression (LIC) achieves state-of-the-art compression performance, yet practical deployments often overlook latency and energy - critical constraints for on-device pipelines and bandwidth-limited applications such as drones and satellite imaging. We address this gap with a codec-aware heterogeneous deployment partitioned at the codec's natural bottleneck - the quantised latent - and mapped across devices: large analysis/synthesis transforms to the GPU (high parallel throughput), the compact, pipelined hyperprior to the FPGA (low-power dataflow), and entropy coding to the CPU. The system remains bit-exact with the reference codec and integrates directly with pretrained CompressAI models via exported ONNX subgraphs.

### Q-realign: Piggybacking Realignment on Quantization for Safe and Efficient LLM Deployment

Public large language models (LLMs) are typically safety-aligned during pretraining, yet task-specific fine-tuning required for deployment often erodes this alignment and introduces safety risks. Existing defenses either embed safety recovery into fine-tuning or rely on fine-tuning-derived priors for post-hoc correction, leaving safety recovery tightly coupled with training and incurring high computational overhead and a complex workflow. To address these challenges, we propose \texttt{Q-realign}, a post-hoc defense method based on post-training quantization, guided by an analysis of representational structure. By reframing quantization as a dual-objective procedure for compression and safety, \texttt{Q-realign} decouples safety alignment from fine-tuning and naturally piggybacks into modern deployment pipelines. Experiments across multiple models and datasets demonstrate that our method substantially reduces unsafe behaviors while preserving task performance, with significant reductions in memory usage and GPU hours. Notably, our approach can recover the safety alignment of a fine-tuned 7B LLM on a single RTX 4090 within 40 minutes. Overall, our work provides a practical, turnkey solution for safety-aware deployment.

We address these gaps with an energy-saving framework that combines structured compression, KD, and low-bit quantization under a differentiable, device-specific energy surrogate. The surrogate predicts latency and energy as differentiable functions of model structure and precision configuration, learned from sparse profiling samples on the target platforms. This design enables end-to-end optimization that directly couples accuracy with hardware costs, rather than relying on proxy metrics or expensive discrete search loops. Our framework trains a compressed student supernet and supports progressive specialization across a family of candidate subnetworks, inspired by the idea of training once and specializing for diverse deployment constraints [6]. Distillation stabilizes learning under reduced capacity and quantization noise, and mixed-precision decisions are treated as optimization variables rather than fixed post-processing choices. In scenarios where calibration data is limited, we draw on ideas from data-free and zero-shot quantization to reduce reliance on large calibration sets during deployment [7]. Motivated by these findings, our framework treats per-layer bit-width as a first-class decision variable tied to predicted device cost, rather than forcing uniform precision or applying quantization as a final step. Finally, because our target is real deployment rather than only benchmark reporting, we emphasize constraints that often determine whether a model is usable in practice: memory headroom, thermal limits, and stability under background load. The differentiable surrogate and multi-objective formulation allow these constraints to be encoded and optimized directly, reducing the risk of selecting models that appear efficient under proxy metrics but fail under real device execution.

Our contributions are as follows:

  * Unified method: We propose a Green AI-oriented framework that jointly integrates structured compression, KD, and mixed-precision low-bit quantization for edge deployment, coordinated by a differentiable objective that targets accuracy, latency, and energy.

  * Differentiable hardware feedback: We introduce a device-specific, differentiable energy surrogate trained from sparse profiling, enabling end-to-end optimization without expensive discrete measurement loops at every training step.

  * Budget-aware deployment selection: We design a multi-objective selection strategy that produces Pareto-efficient configurations for Raspberry Pi and Jetson Nano, supporting controllable trade-offs under explicit latency and energy budgets.

  * Method performance: On Raspberry Pi, our approach achieves 79.7% top-1 on ImageNet-1k while reducing latency from 84 ms to 58 ms and energy from 505 mJ to 330 mJ compared with a strong PTQ baseline, and improves over an on-device NAS baseline at 64 ms and 380 mJ; we also achieve 95.7% at 14.2 ms and 78 mJ on CIFAR-10, and 95.1% at 4.3 ms and 19 mJ on Speech Commands.

SECTION II.

In contrast, our framework embeds compression choices into a device-aware optimization loop that explicitly models accuracy, latency, and energy on the target edge platform.

### C. Quantization and Knowledge Distillation for Edge Inference

Quantization is central for edge deployment because integer arithmetic can reduce memory traffic and accelerate kernels, but accuracy can degrade without careful training and calibration. Foundational pipelines established quantization-aware training (QAT) for integer-only inference, demonstrating that appropriate fake quantization and scaling strategies can preserve accuracy [22]. Despite strong accuracy, QAT requires access to the full training set and a non-trivial retraining budget, which motivates PTQ approaches for deployment scenarios with limited resources. Mixed-precision approaches automate bit-width assignment with hardware feedback, improving latency and energy efficiency relative to uniform precision baselines [23]. Training-time activation quantization methods such as parameterized clipping (PACT) [24] improve stability when pushing weights and activations to very low precision, while learned step size quantization (LSQ) [25] directly optimizes quantizer parameters to achieve strong low-bit accuracy. For deployment settings with limited calibration data, data-free quantization (DFQ) techniques rely on weight equalization and bias correction to mitigate accuracy loss without retraining [26], and post-training schemes such as BRECQ [27] reconstruct network blocks to extend PTQ toward lower bit-widths. Recent work on activation-aware weight quantization (AWQ) [28] demonstrates that protecting a small fraction of salient weights from aggressive quantization can greatly reduce perplexity degradation, and 4-bit quantization of speech recognition models [29] shows that these ideas transfer to edge audio tasks. Orthogonally, contrastive representation distillation (CRD) [30] improves compact student models by transferring richer structural information beyond output logits, suggesting that KD and quantization should be considered jointly when the goal is efficient, accurate edge inference. Our framework builds on these foundations but uniquely couples them to a hardware-profiling surrogate, ensuring that quantization bit-width decisions directly minimize measured device energy rather than serving as standalone accuracy-preservation techniques.
Future work can extend this direction by incorporating additional system signals (temperature, dynamic frequency scaling) into the surrogate, exploring multi-device surrogates that generalize across hardware classes, and coupling energy-aware objectives with compiler-level optimizations such as operator fusion and kernel selection—a promising path to further reduce the gap between predicted and realized efficiency.

SECTION V.

## Conclusion

This work targets sustainable deployment of deep learning by addressing the practical gap between accuracy-centric training and energy-constrained edge inference. We presented an integrated framework combining structured compression, KD, and low-bit quantization, and introduced a differentiable, device-specific energy surrogate to jointly optimize accuracy, latency, and energy within a unified training pipeline. Our primary novelty is the tight integration of these established mechanisms under a surrogate-driven feedback loop that couples training-time decisions to deployment-time hardware costs. Experiments on Raspberry Pi and Jetson Nano across vision and audio benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly reduces inference energy and latency while maintaining competitive accuracy, and that these gains remain stable under ablations, robustness stress tests, and consistent across both target platforms. Beyond improving efficiency, the framework provides controllable budget-aware model selection, enabling practitioners to choose operating points that meet deployment constraints without extensive trial-and- error profiling. Future work will explore broader hardware generalization of the surrogate, tighter integration with compiler-level optimizations, and adaptive policies that respond to dynamic runtime conditions such as temperature and frequency scaling.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
